pebbles.title: Summer surface temperature from Landsat, against the city's average

narration.short: Surface temperature within 150 m of this address against the city's land average, from clear summer Landsat images.

provenance.source_name: Landsat 8 and 9 Collection 2 Level 2 surface temperature (USGS), via Microsoft Planetary Computer
provenance.citation: Landsat Collection 2 Level 2 Science Products, surface temperature band (USGS EROS), Landsat 8 and 9, WRS row 032, Tier 1 scenes of 1 June to 10 September with at least 95% of the city's land clear. Riprap averages 30 m pixels into 90 m cells and reports each cell against the city's land mean in the same image (scripts/bake_surface_temperature.py; the images are listed in data/heat/surface_temp.json).

heat_surface.narrative: Landsat measured the surface of the ground within 150 m of this address at 7.5°F warmer than the city's land average, over 18 clear summer images from 2023-07-23 to 2026-08-08, each taken at about 11:35 am Eastern Daylight Time; image by image it ran from 5.5 to 9.2°F warmer. In the latest image, on 2026-08-08, the surface here read 105.2°F against a city average of 97.9°F. This is the temperature of roofs, pavement and treetops seen from orbit on clear late mornings, not the air temperature a person feels.

hvi.narrative: The NYC Health Department's Heat Vulnerability Index (2023, from 2016 to 2020 data) scores Jamaica, the neighbourhood around this address, at 5 out of 5, the highest risk group. The index ranks neighbourhoods against each other by a model of heat deaths, from surface temperature, green space, air conditioning, income and the share of Black residents; it is not a measurement of heat at an address, and the department notes that every neighbourhood has residents at risk, whatever its score. For Jamaica the department lists 84.9% of households with air conditioning and 14.7% green space.

heat_visits.narrative: Residents of Queens community district 12 made 79 emergency department visits for heat illness in May to September of 2018 to 2022, an age-adjusted rate of 7.6 per 100,000 a year against 6.0 citywide (NYC Health Department, from state hospital records). Visits are counted by where the patient lives, and only when diagnosed as heat illness.

city_landcover.narrative: New York City's 2017 land cover map (6 inch, from LiDAR and aerial imagery) shows that 83.5% of the ground within 500 m of this address is paved or built over and 16.5% is green (11.5% tree canopy).

landcover.narrative: Experimental: a satellite land-cover model estimates that 83.7% of the ground within 500 m of this address is paved or built over and 16.0% is green (9.5% tree canopy), on Sentinel-2 scenes from 2026; no change between years is read from it. Limits: it estimates the share of each 10 m satellite pixel that is canopy, grass, paving, roof, water or bare ground, learned from the city's 2017 six-inch map, so detail finer than about 30 m is blurred and a tree over a street counts as canopy; against the city's own 2021 six-inch map, on squares it never trained on, it read a typical district's paved share 1.7 points above the map's (at most 7.8 points off in the 46 districts with enough test ground) and its mean error per land-cover group was 4.8 points at best, more than the 3.0 points of the city's 2017 map read as if it were 2021, so the 2017 map is the more accurate source for its year; two images of one summer differ by under 2.0 points in a district's paved share 19 times in 20, but between 2018 and 2024 the shares of 49 of 59 districts differ by more, so its maps of different years are not compared. Rely on NYC's own land cover maps (2017 and 2021, 6 inch) and building footprints for a survey.

heat_obs.narrative: The air at JFK Airport, the nearest weather station (7.8 km away), was 72°F at 10:20 on 2026-10-02, with a heat index of 72°F. This is the station's reading, not this address's.

heat_station.narrative: At JFK Airport, the nearest long-record weather station (7.8 km away), the air temperature reached 90°F on 10 days in 2026 through 2026-10-01 and on 15 in 2025; the 1991 to 2020 average is 11 a year. The highest reading of 2026 was 102°F on 2026-07-02. These are the station's readings, not this address's.
heat_station.headline_value: 10 days at 90°F or above in 2026 (JFK Airport)

cool_features.narrative: NYC Parks lists spray showers at 2 parks or playgrounds within 800 m of this address (lists updated 2026-09-03 and 2026-09-15); the nearest is the spray shower at Harvard Playground, 386 m away. Spray showers and outdoor pools run in summer only, and the list does not say whether one is working today. Cooling centers are separate: the city opens them only during a heat emergency and lists them then at finder.nyc.gov/coolingcenters (or call 311).

nws_heat_alerts.narrative: No active NWS heat advisory, watch or warning at this point, checked 2026-10-02 14:40 UTC.

nws_heat_forecast.narrative: Over the next 7 days the National Weather Service expects daytime highs of 82°F today, 70°F Saturday, 66°F Sunday, 69°F Monday, 61°F Tuesday, 62°F Wednesday, 67°F Thursday in the 2.5 km grid cell around this place (issued 2026-10-02 07:47 Eastern); the highest apparent temperature it gives, which is the heat index when it is hot, is 85°F on Friday October 2. The Weather Service's New York office issues a Heat Advisory when it expects the heat index to reach 95°F for two days in a row or 100°F at any time, and an Extreme Heat Warning at 105°F for two hours. The Weather Service wrote this for an area; it is not a prediction for a building.
nws_heat_forecast.headline_value: high of 82°F forecast in the next week

npcc4_heat.narrative: NPCC4 (2024) projects 38 to 62 days a year at or above 90°F in New York City by the 2050s and 46 to 85 by the 2080s, as its middle range (25th to 75th percentile), against 17 a year in 1981-2010; the 90th percentile is 69 days by the 2050s and 108 by the 2080s. Days at or above 95°F go from 4 a year to 14 to 32 by the 2050s, and heat waves from 2 a year to 5 to 8. These figures are for the city as a whole, not for a neighbourhood.
